name: Liam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dr Rahman. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Liam's fine. I'm at Hollins Road Health Centre by quarter to eight, and the first thing I do is open the inbox: blood results, hospital letters, repeat prescriptions. There are usually ninety to a hundred and twenty things in it before I've taken my coat off. Morning surgery starts at half eight, eighteen patients at ten minutes each, which in practice means I'm twenty minutes behind by ten o'clock. Then home visits, which I actually love, then afternoon surgery, then the phone calls I promised people. I'm out the door around seven, and I finish the inbox at the kitchen table once Zara and Sami are in bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is knowing people over years. I've been at Hollins Road eleven years, so I've done the six-week baby checks on children who are now starting school, and I know which of my older patients say “I'm fine” when they're not. There's a man, Mr Kowalczyk, eighty-one, with heart failure, who books every second Tuesday whether he needs to or not, and it took me two years to work out that Tuesday was the day his wife died. What wears me out is the clicking. For every ten minutes with a person there's about five minutes of forms, codes and letters, and that's the bit that eats my evenings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at work at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The clinic signed up last year for an AI note-taker. It listens to the appointment, with the patient's permission, and drafts the notes for me. I use it two or three days a week, mostly on busy Mondays. Tom, our nurse practitioner, swears by it, and Dr Oduya, our senior partner, won't touch it. I'm in the middle: it saves me maybe ten minutes an afternoon, but I check every line, because last month it wrote down a penicillin allergy for a woman when it was her sister who had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I say at the practice meeting now: it's a useful tool, check its work, and don't let it near anything you can't explain. Online I wouldn't say much at all. Doctors who post about the future of medicine tend to regret it. To friends I'd joke that maybe I'll get home before nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. Relieved because my job looks the same and the mortgage gets paid. Disappointed because the bit I hate, the inbox and the letters, would still be sitting there, and I'd half hoped something would finally take it off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much different. I'd probably use the note-taker every day instead of two or three, once Tom and the others have ironed out the mistakes. I might do one of the free online courses the health board puts on, a couple of evenings. And we'd keep putting about two hundred a month into savings, like we do now. We've got roughly four months of bills put by, and I'd like it to be six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like a Tuesday. There's something comforting about a future that looks like more of the same, even when the same is tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd half hoped something would take the inbox off you. If you could hand one task to a machine tomorrow, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital letters. I get a four-page discharge letter, and somewhere on page three it says “please increase the water tablet and recheck kidney function in one week”. If I miss that line, it's my problem. A machine that pulled out the one sentence I actually have to act on would give me back an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And who at the clinic would notice the difference least?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise on reception, which is funny, because she works hardest of all of us. Her day starts with the phones at eight o'clock: sixty people trying to get twelve same-day appointments. A better search engine doesn't help her tell a frightened mum there's nothing until Thursday. In this picture Denise's job is exactly as hard as it is now.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, so check its work and don't let it near anything you can't explain. I'd keep quiet online, because doctors who post about the future of medicine tend to regret it, and I'd joke to friends that maybe I'll get home before nine.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. My job looks the same and the mortgage gets paid, but the inbox and the hospital letters I hate would still be there.
S0.do: Uses the clinic's AI note-taker every day instead of two or three days a week, once colleagues have ironed out the mistakes. Takes a free online course from the health board over a couple of evenings, and keeps saving about two hundred a month to grow four months of bills to six.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of tiredness. A future that looks like more of the same is comforting, even if the same is exhausting.
S0.quote: A machine that pulled out the one sentence I actually have to act on would give me back an hour a day.
S0.fieldNote: Liam's first reaction wasn't fear but a wish list: he wants AI to take the paperwork, not the patients. He's careful about speaking in public and said plainly that doctors who post about the future tend to regret it. Asked who'd notice least, he went straight to Denise on reception, whose hardest moments no search tool would touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the practice I'd say it's the best of both worlds: we get time to test things properly before they touch patients. Medicine is slow anyway. It took us four years to stop faxing the hospital. At the school gate I'd tell people their family doctor isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bit that bothers me is “fewer beginners”. We had a trainee last year, Aisha, and half of what she learned, she learned doing the boring stuff: the letters, the results, the repeat prescriptions. If the machine does the boring stuff, how does the next Aisha learn when a normal blood test isn't normal for this patient? For me personally, I'm forty-three. Ten slow years takes me to fifty-three, and I think I can ride that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up to be the person at Hollins Road who tests the new tools. Not because I'm a fan, but because Dr Oduya won't and Tom would sign up for anything, so somebody in the middle should do it. I'd keep going to the monthly training afternoons. Money-wise, nothing dramatic. We'd probably stop Sami's extra maths tutor, that's forty a week, and put it into savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low hum of worry, mostly for other people. For me it feels manageable, like a slow leak in a tyre you can keep pumping up on the way to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Aisha. If she rang you in this world and asked whether to stay in family medicine, what would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her yes, stay, but learn to argue with the machine. The doctors who do well will be the ones who can look at a confident answer on a screen and say, “No, I've met this woman, and she doesn't complain unless something's really wrong.” I'd also tell her to write some of her own letters by hand for a year, the way I learned to take a blood pressure with a cuff before we had the automatic ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can ride out ten years, but you'd also drop the tutor and save more. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I believe I'll be fine, and I'm also the son of a man who ran a corner shop and always kept three months' rent in a biscuit tin behind the counter. You can be confident and still keep the biscuit tin.

S1.say: It's the best of both worlds, because we get time to test things properly before they touch patients. Medicine is slow anyway, and I'd tell people at the school gate that their family doctor isn't going anywhere.
S1.think: The part that bothers me is fewer beginners, because trainees like Aisha learn from the boring work a machine would take. For me personally, ten slow years takes me to fifty-three, and I think I can ride that.
S1.do: Volunteers to be the person at the clinic who tests new AI tools, as the middle ground between a colleague who refuses them and one who'd try anything. Keeps going to the monthly training afternoons and drops his son's forty-a-week maths tutor to put that money into savings.
S1.feel: A low hum of worry, mostly on behalf of young doctors and others. For himself it feels manageable, like a slow leak he can keep topping up.
S1.quote: You can be confident and still keep the biscuit tin.
S1.fieldNote: His worry in this picture is about training, not his own job: he kept coming back to Aisha and how young doctors learn from dull work. There's a small gap between saying he can ride it out and cutting the maths tutor to save more, which he explained through his father's corner shop. He sees himself as the sensible tester, standing between an enthusiast and a refuser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is mostly an admin story, not a medicine story, and that the clinic has to look after the people it affects. In public I'd keep out of the politics completely. My patients vote every way you can think of, and they all need a doctor they can trust on Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this is the one where Hollins Road changes most and my bit changes least. Gary, our practice manager, already has a spreadsheet of what the admin team costs. If an AI can do the coding, the letters and the booking, three or four of our nine admin staff are gone. And the honest, selfish thought is that I'd quite like to lose the paperwork, even if the price is somebody I've worked beside for eleven years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the first partners' meeting I'd argue for moving admin staff into jobs like patient navigators, people who walk patients through the system, instead of just letting them go. I'd use the AI assistant for all my letters and results and give the hour back to longer appointments for my frailest patients. At home, our mortgage deal ends next spring, so I'd fix the rate for five years rather than gamble on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty. I'd be getting the thing I've moaned about for years, and other people would be paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the week Gary tells the admin team. What happens at lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We eat in the back room where the old paper notes used to be, and Denise always brings too much rice and makes us take some. If Gary told them on a Monday, I think that Tuesday nobody would take the rice, and that's how I'd know it was serious. Denise is fifty-six. She isn't going to retrain for one of these new AI jobs, whatever they turn out to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd quite like to lose the paperwork. How do you hold that next to Denise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I'd want both: the machine doing the forms, and Denise staying to do what she's really good at, which is knowing that when Mrs Achebe rings and says it's “nothing urgent”, it's urgent. Whether the practice can afford both isn't up to me, and I'd hate that it isn't up to me.

S2.say: This is mostly an admin story, not a medicine story, and the clinic has to look after the people it affects. I'd keep out of the politics in public, because my patients vote every way and they all need a doctor they can trust.
S2.think: This is the one where the clinic changes most and my own work changes least, with three or four of nine admin staff likely gone. Selfishly, I'd quite like to lose the paperwork, even if the price is a colleague of eleven years.
S2.do: Argues at the first partners' meeting for moving admin staff into roles like patient navigators instead of laying them off. Uses the AI assistant for all his letters and results, putting the saved hour into longer appointments for frail patients, and fixes the mortgage rate for five years when the deal ends next spring.
S2.feel: Uneasy and a little guilty. He'd finally get rid of the paperwork he's complained about for years, but colleagues would pay the price.
S2.quote: If Gary told them on a Monday, I think that Tuesday nobody would take the rice, and that's how I'd know it was serious.
S2.fieldNote: This was the first scenario where Liam admitted a selfish wish, wanting the paperwork gone, and he didn't dress it up. He measured the change through the people at the lunch table rather than through numbers. He was firm about staying out of politics in public because his patients vote every way, and he disliked that decisions about Denise wouldn't be his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I think most doctors would say: an AI that's as good as a doctor on paper still needs a doctor in the room, and patients want a person. I'd say it calmly, too. People would be scared, and a frightened family doctor doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where it touches me. I'm a good doctor, but I'm not the best diagnostician in the building. Dr Oduya is. If a machine matches skilled professionals at thinking, it's at least as good as me at the thinking part. What it can't do is the knowing-people part. A machine can read the blood test. It can't tell that Mr Kowalczyk only comes in because Tuesday is the day his wife died. My worry is whether the people who pay for clinics see that difference, or just see the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Hannah at the kitchen table with the bank statements, which we both hate doing. We'd cancel the summer week at the coast, that's about two and a half thousand, and try to get from four months' savings to eight. At work I'd ask the partners to make me lead for home visits and the two care homes we cover, because that's the work where you need a body in the room. I'd want to be holding that work when the budget meeting comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the night before an exam I haven't revised for. Not panic. Just a cold feeling that being a decent, ordinary doctor might not be enough anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Zara and Sami about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zara's twelve, and she'd ask me straight out whether a computer is going to be the doctor now. I'd tell her the truth: computers are getting very clever, Dad's job will change, and we'll be fine because Mum and I have a plan. Then I'd go downstairs and check the plan was real. Sami's nine. He'd just want to know if the computer can do his maths homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: House prices boom in this picture. Does that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper. Our house on Larch Avenue would be worth more, but we'd only see that money if we sold and moved somewhere cheaper, and everywhere would be dearer too. What I'd actually feel is the other side of it: patients who rent and just lost office jobs, coming in with chest pains that turn out to be panic about the rent.

S3.say: An AI that's as good as a doctor on paper still needs a doctor in the room, and patients want a person. I'd say it calmly, because people would be scared and a frightened family doctor doesn't help anyone.
S3.think: I'm a good doctor but not the best diagnostician, so a machine would be at least as good as me at the thinking part. It can't know people the way I do, but I worry the people who pay for clinics will only see the price.
S3.do: Sits down with his partner in the first month to go through the bank statements, cancels the summer week at the coast (about two and a half thousand) and aims to grow savings from four months to eight. Asks the partners to make him lead for home visits and the two care homes the clinic covers, so he holds hands-on work before budget talks.
S3.feel: A cold, unprepared feeling, like the night before an exam he hasn't revised for. Not panic, but real doubt that being a decent, ordinary doctor will be enough.
S3.quote: Just a cold feeling that being a decent, ordinary doctor might not be enough anymore.
S3.fieldNote: This is where Liam's view of himself as an average doctor started to matter: he named Dr Oduya as the better diagnostician without being asked. His defence is the knowing-people part of the job, and his Mr Kowalczyk story was the most vivid moment of the interview. He reached for the home visits and care homes as safe ground, which set up his reaction to the next card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say care homes need people. A robot that lifts Mrs Ferreira out of bed without hurting her back or its own is fine, as long as somebody still sits with her afterwards. I'd say that at a health board meeting, though, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the care homes that get me, because I'd just told you I'd shelter in them. In the last picture you needed a body in the room. In this one, some of the bodies in the room are machines, and the carers I work with lose out first. My own job is still hands-on in a way a robot isn't yet: pressing on a sore belly, holding someone's hand while I tell them it's cancer. But everyone around me is losing ground, and so are my patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in counselling skills, about four hundred in fees, because I think half my list would be people who'd lost their work and their sense of who they are, and I'm not trained enough for that. I'd keep pushing the savings toward eight months. And Hannah and I would finally write the wills we've been meaning to write for six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's like watching a flood come up the street when your house happens to be on the one bit of high ground. That's the one I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the care homes would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace at Elmfield. She's sixty, works nights, and sends part of her pay to her grandchildren. She's the one who rings me at three in the morning and says, “Doctor, he's not right,” and she's always correct. If a robot does the turning and lifting, the home might keep one Grace instead of four, and I don't know which one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own job is still hands-on, but you sound more worried here than in the last picture. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a family doctor is only as healthy as the town around him. When the biscuit factory on Mill Lane closed, the year I started at Hollins Road, I saw what happened: the drinking, the blood pressures, the sixteen-year-olds with nothing to do. In this picture I'd be safe and busy in the worst way. I didn't train to be the last man standing.

S4.say: Care homes need people, and a robot that lifts a resident out of bed is fine as long as somebody still sits with her afterwards. I'd say that at a health board meeting rather than online.
S4.think: The care homes I planned to shelter in are exactly where the robots arrive, and the carers I work with lose out first. My own hands-on work is safe for now, but everyone around me is losing ground, and so are my patients.
S4.do: Signs up for an evening course in counselling skills, about four hundred in fees, expecting many patients who've lost their work. Keeps pushing savings toward eight months and finally writes wills with his partner after six years of putting it off.
S4.feel: Heavy, like watching a flood come up the street while his own house sits on high ground. This is the picture he'd lose sleep over.
S4.quote: In this picture I'd be safe and busy in the worst way. I didn't train to be the last man standing.
S4.fieldNote: The surprise here is that Liam is most distressed in the picture where his own job is safest. His fear is about his town and the carers around him, shaped by what he saw after the biscuit factory on Mill Lane closed. He noticed for himself that his care-home plan from the last card no longer works, and moved straight to retraining for the mental health load he expects.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots one, even though it's the one where my own job is safest. What would help is the health board deciding now, before it happens, that machines take the paperwork and the lifting, and the money saved goes on people: more carers, more Denises, longer appointments. If I had twenty minutes with each patient instead of ten, I'd welcome every machine you could build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what patients want, and that's the question I'd ask. Mr Kowalczyk would take a robot to carry his shopping up the stairs tomorrow. He'd never take one in place of the doctor who knows about Tuesdays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you, Liam. That's everything I needed.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No problem. I've got about forty results waiting for me, so a machine that did those would be welcome right now.

headlineQuote: A machine can read the blood test. It can't tell that Mr Kowalczyk only comes in because Tuesday is the day his wife died.
portrait: Liam Rahman is a 43-year-old family doctor who has spent eleven years at a busy local clinic, with a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of savings. He's a careful middle-of-the-road user of AI who wants machines to take the inbox and the hospital letters, not the patients. Through the first three pictures he stays fairly steady, saving a little more and positioning himself as the doctor who tests new tools and does the home visits, though he admits he's an ordinary diagnostician who might not be enough if AI matches professionals. His sharpest worry comes in the robots picture, where his own job is safest but the carers, admin staff and patients around him lose ground. What drives him is knowing people over years, like the patient who books every second Tuesday.
biggestWorry: The robots picture worries him most, even though his own job is safest there, because his colleagues, the care-home carers and his patients would all be losing their work around him.
whatWouldHelp: He wants the health board to decide in advance that machines take the paperwork and the lifting and that the money saved goes on people: more carers, more reception staff and longer appointments. With twenty minutes per patient instead of ten, he says he'd welcome every machine.
